Overview — The Male Gonad’s Two Jobs

The testis does two things at once: it makes sperm (an exocrine, spermatogenic role) inside the seminiferous tubules, and it makes testosterone (an endocrine role) from the Leydig cells in the surrounding interstitium.

🔬 Image slot — testis at low power — packed seminiferous tubules with germinal epithelium, separated by interstitium containing Leydig cells
  • A dense capsule, the tunica albuginea, sends septa in to divide the testis into lobules.
  • Each lobule holds 1–4 coiled seminiferous tubules that drain into the rete testis → epididymis.
Two compartments, two cell families: the tubule (Sertoli + germ cells → sperm) and the interstitium (Leydig cells → testosterone).
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — seminiferous tubule cross-sections — stratified germinal epithelium, tall Sertoli cells, and clusters of eosinophilic Leydig cells between tubules
  • Seminiferous tubules cut in cross-section, lined by a thick, stratified germinal (spermatogenic) epithelium.
  • A lumen containing tails of spermatozoa in active tubules.
  • Leydig cells — clusters of eosinophilic cells in the interstitium between tubules.
  • Sertoli cells — tall columnar cells spanning the epithelium, with a pale nucleus and a prominent nucleolus.
Seminiferous tubules + interstitial Leydig cells → testis. The stratified germ-cell layers maturing toward a sperm-filled lumen are unmistakable.
The Seminiferous Tubule & Spermatogenesis
🔬 Image slot — spermatogenic sequence — spermatogonia at the base maturing through spermatocytes and spermatids to luminal spermatozoa

Germ cells mature from the basement membrane toward the lumen:

1
Spermatogoniadiploid stem cells at the base
2
Primary spermatocyteslargest cells; undergo meiosis I
3
Secondary spermatocytes → spermatidsmeiosis II; haploid, short-lived
4
Spermatozoaspermiogenesis → released into lumen
Primary spermatocytes are the largest, most conspicuous germ cells (their condensed meiotic chromatin stands out). Spermiogenesis is the final remodelling of round spermatids into streamlined spermatozoa.
Sertoli Cells & the Blood–Testis Barrier
  • Tall columnar cells extending from basement membrane to lumen; they support and nourish the germ cells.
  • Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells form the blood–testis barrier, splitting the epithelium into a basal (spermatogonia) and an adluminal (meiotic cells) compartment.
  • They phagocytose residual bodies and secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP), inhibin, and (in the fetus) anti-Müllerian hormone.
  • FSH acts on Sertoli cells; inhibin feeds back to suppress FSH.
The blood–testis barrier keeps developing (haploid) sperm immunologically hidden. If it is breached (trauma, vasectomy, infection) the immune system can form anti-sperm antibodies.
Leydig Cells & Hormonal Control
🔬 Image slot — interstitium — clusters of eosinophilic Leydig cells with lipid droplets and Reinke crystals between the tubules
Leydig cells
  • Interstitial, eosinophilic, lipid-rich; contain Reinke crystals
  • Secrete testosterone under LH control
Sertoli cells
  • Respond to FSH
  • Make ABP (keeps intratubular testosterone high) & inhibin
LH → Leydig → testosterone; FSH → Sertoli. High local testosterone (bound to ABP) plus FSH together drive spermatogenesis; inhibin and testosterone provide negative feedback.
The Duct System — From Tubule to Vas
🔬 Image slot — excurrent ducts — rete testis, ciliated efferent ductules, and the epididymis with stereocilia
1
Straight tubules → rete testisSertoli-only tubuli recti into a network in the mediastinum
2
Efferent ductulesciliated; reabsorb testicular fluid (scalloped lining)
3
Epididymispseudostratified columnar with stereocilia; sperm mature & are stored
4
Vas deferensthick three-layer smooth muscle
Epididymis = pseudostratified columnar epithelium with long stereocilia and a smooth luminal border of stored sperm — a classic slide.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Cryptorchidism
Undescended testis → impaired spermatogenesis and increased germ-cell tumour risk
Testicular torsion
Twisted spermatic cord → ischaemia; a surgical emergency (sudden pain, high-riding testis)
Seminoma
Commonest germ-cell tumour; sheets of clear “fried-egg” cells with a lymphocytic stroma; may raise LDH/hCG
Non-seminomatous GCTs
Yolk-sac (↑AFP), choriocarcinoma (↑hCG), embryonal carcinoma, teratoma
Klinefelter (47,XXY)
Small firm testes with hyalinised tubules & Leydig hyperplasia → infertility
Varicocele
Dilated pampiniform plexus (“bag of worms”), usually left; a cause of infertility
Mumps orchitis and Sertoli-cell-only syndrome (germ-cell aplasia → tubules lined by Sertoli cells only) are classic causes of azoospermia/infertility.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Seminiferous tubules + interstitial Leydig cells = testis.
Germ cells mature base → lumen: spermatogonia → primary spermatocyte (largest) → spermatid → spermatozoon.
Sertoli cells: support + blood–testis barrier (tight junctions); FSH target; secrete ABP, inhibin, AMH.
Leydig cells: interstitial, eosinophilic, Reinke crystals; secrete testosterone under LH.
LH → Leydig → testosterone; FSH → Sertoli; inhibin feeds back on FSH.
Epididymis = pseudostratified columnar with stereocilia; sperm mature & are stored there.
Seminoma = commonest, fried-egg cells + lymphocytic stroma; yolk-sac → AFP, choriocarcinoma → hCG.
Cryptorchidism raises germ-cell tumour risk; Klinefelter = hyalinised tubules & infertility.

Overview — The Female Gonad

The ovary has two roles: producing oocytes (oogenesis) and making the sex hormones oestrogen and progesterone. Its structure is a follicle-packed cortex around a vascular medulla.

🔬 Image slot — ovary at low power — cortex containing follicles at different stages around a central vascular medulla, with a surface epithelium
  • The surface is covered by a simple cuboidal “germinal” epithelium (a misnomer) over the tunica albuginea.
  • The cortex holds the follicles; the medulla carries vessels, lymphatics and nerves.
Everything examinable happens in the cortex: follicles maturing, ovulating, and regressing into a corpus luteum and then a corpus albicans.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — ovarian cortex — primordial, primary and antral follicles, a corpus luteum and a corpus albicans, under a cuboidal surface epithelium
  • Follicles at multiple stages crowded in the cortex — the diagnostic feature.
  • A simple cuboidal surface epithelium over the tunica albuginea.
  • A large, folded corpus luteum and/or a white fibrous corpus albicans scar.
A cortex full of follicles at different stages → ovary. Grade the follicle by its granulosa layer and whether an antrum has formed.
Folliculogenesis — Grading the Follicle
🔬 Image slot — follicle stages — primordial, primary (zona pellucida), secondary antral (theca), and Graafian follicle with cumulus oophorus
Primordial follicle
Primary oocyte + a single layer of flat (squamous) follicular cells; the resting pool
Primary follicle
Single (then multiple) layer of cuboidal granulosa cells; zona pellucida appears; theca begins to form
Secondary (antral) follicle
A fluid-filled antrum appears; theca interna & externa defined; Call–Exner bodies in granulosa
Graafian (mature) follicle
Large antrum; oocyte on a cumulus oophorus with its corona radiata, poised to ovulate
Read two things: the granulosa layer (flat = primordial; cuboidal = primary) and the antrum (present = secondary/Graafian). The zona pellucida is a glycoprotein shell around the oocyte for sperm binding.
The Two-Cell, Two-Gonadotropin Model
Theca interna — LH
  • LH drives production of androgens (androstenedione)
  • Androgens diffuse into the granulosa
Granulosa — FSH
  • FSH induces aromatase → converts androgens to oestrogen
  • Also secretes inhibin (feeds back on FSH)
Theca makes the androgen (LH); granulosa aromatises it to oestrogen (FSH). This division of labour is the two-cell, two-gonadotropin model — and explains why aromatase inhibitors and gonadotropins work where they do.
Ovulation, Corpus Luteum & Corpus Albicans
🔬 Image slot — corpus luteum — folded wall of large pale granulosa lutein cells and smaller peripheral theca lutein cells; adjacent white corpus albicans
1
LH surge → ovulationreleases the secondary oocyte (arrested in metaphase II)
2
Corpus luteumgranulosa + theca lutein cells → progesterone
3
Corpus albicanswhite fibrous scar if no pregnancy (~14 days)
  • The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and oestrogen) to maintain the endometrium.
  • No pregnancy → it regresses to a corpus albicans; pregnancy → hCG rescues it as the corpus luteum of pregnancy.
  • Most follicles never ovulate — they undergo atresia at any stage.
Corpus luteum = progesterone factory; corpus albicans = its white scar. hCG from a pregnancy keeps the corpus luteum alive until the placenta takes over.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Polycystic ovary syndrome
Multiple subcapsular follicular cysts, thickened tunica, arrested follicles; anovulation + hyperandrogenism
Serous cystadeno(carcinoma)
Commonest ovarian epithelial tumour; psammoma bodies; raised CA-125
Mature teratoma (dermoid)
Germ-cell tumour with tissues from all three layers (hair, skin, teeth); usually benign
Granulosa cell tumour
Sex-cord tumour; Call–Exner bodies; secretes oestrogen & inhibin → precocious puberty / endometrial hyperplasia
Sertoli–Leydig / fibroma
Sertoli–Leydig → androgens (virilisation); fibroma → Meigs syndrome (ascites + pleural effusion)
Endometrioma
Endometriosis in the ovary forming a “chocolate cyst” of old blood
Tumour markers: serous epithelial → CA-125; yolk-sac → AFP; granulosa cell → inhibin; dysgerminoma (the female seminoma) → LDH/hCG.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Cortex full of follicles at various stages + cuboidal surface epithelium = ovary.
Primordial (flat granulosa) → primary (cuboidal + zona pellucida) → secondary/antral (antrum + theca) → Graafian (cumulus oophorus).
Two-cell model: theca (LH → androgen) + granulosa (FSH → aromatase → oestrogen).
Zona pellucida = glycoprotein sperm-binding shell; corona radiata = granulosa around the ovulated oocyte.
LH surge → ovulation; corpus luteum → progesterone; corpus albicans = white scar.
hCG rescues the corpus luteum in pregnancy; most follicles undergo atresia.
Granulosa cell tumour: Call–Exner bodies + oestrogen/inhibin; Sertoli–Leydig → androgens; fibroma → Meigs.
Serous cystadenocarcinoma = commonest, psammoma bodies, CA-125; PCOS = peripheral cysts + hyperandrogenism.

Overview — A Three-Layered Muscular Organ

The uterus houses and nourishes the embryo. Its wall has three layers, but the examinable action is all in the endometrium, which is remodelled every month by ovarian hormones.

🔬 Image slot — uterine wall — endometrium with glands in stroma, thick myometrium of smooth muscle, and outer perimetrium
1
Endometriummucosa — glands + stroma; cycles monthly
2
Myometriumthick interlacing smooth muscle
3
Perimetriumouter serosa / adventitia
The endometrium has two layers: a stratum functionalis that is shed and rebuilt each cycle, and a stratum basalis that stays put and regenerates it.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — endometrium — simple columnar surface epithelium, tubular endometrial glands set in a cellular stroma, over thick myometrium
  • Endometrial glands (simple columnar) embedded in a cellular stroma — the diagnostic mucosa.
  • A thick myometrium of interlacing smooth-muscle bundles beneath it.
  • The gland shape and stroma tell you the cycle phase (straight vs coiled glands).
Endometrial glands in a cellular stroma over a thick myometrium → uterus. Then date it: straight tubular glands = proliferative; coiled “sawtooth” glands with secretions = secretory.
The Two Endometrial Layers
Stratum functionalis
  • Superficial; shed at menstruation and rebuilt each cycle
  • Supplied by spiral arteries (hormone-sensitive)
Stratum basalis
  • Deep; retained — regenerates the functionalis
  • Supplied by straight (basal) arteries
Spiral arteries feed the functionalis and are the key to menstruation: when hormones fall they constrict, causing the ischaemia that sheds the layer. The basalis and its straight arteries survive to rebuild.
The Menstrual Cycle Phases
🔬 Image slot — cycle phases — menstrual shedding, proliferative straight glands, and secretory coiled glands with glycogen vacuoles and stromal oedema
Menstrual (days 1–4)
Shedding of the functionalis — fragmented glands, blood and stromal breakdown
Proliferative (days 5–14)
Oestrogen-driven regeneration: straight, narrow tubular glands, abundant mitoses, compact stroma
Secretory (days 15–28)
Progesterone-driven: coiled “sawtooth” glands, glycogen vacuoles, luminal secretions, stromal oedema & spiral-artery growth
Oestrogen builds (proliferative); progesterone matures/secretes (secretory). Ovulation at ~day 14 is the switch; the corpus luteum then supplies the progesterone.
Dating the Endometrium & Why Menstruation Happens
  • Straight tubular glands + mitoses → proliferative (oestrogen).
  • Sub-nuclear glycogen vacuoles (~day 16–17) are the first sign ovulation has occurred.
  • Supra-nuclear secretion → luminal secretions → stromal oedema through the mid-secretory phase.
  • Predecidual change & coiled spiral arteries late (~day 23+).
No fertilisation → the corpus luteum regresses → progesterone & oestrogen fall → spiral arteries constrict → ischaemic shedding of the functionalis = menstruation.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Endometrial hyperplasia
Unopposed oestrogen → increased gland:stroma ratio; atypical hyperplasia is premalignant
Endometrial adenocarcinoma
Commonest gynae cancer; postmenopausal bleeding; risk = unopposed oestrogen, obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen, Lynch
Leiomyoma (fibroid)
Commonest uterine tumour; benign whorled smooth muscle; oestrogen-dependent; menorrhagia
Adenomyosis
Endometrial glands & stroma within the myometrium → bulky, tender uterus
Endometriosis
Endometrial tissue outside the uterus → cyclical pain, adhesions, chocolate cysts
Asherman’s syndrome
Damage to the basalis (over-curettage) → intrauterine adhesions, amenorrhoea, infertility
Leiomyosarcoma is the rare malignant smooth-muscle tumour (high mitoses, necrosis, atypia) — distinct from the common benign leiomyoma.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Endometrial glands in a cellular stroma over a thick myometrium = uterus.
Functionalis (shed; spiral arteries) vs basalis (regenerates; straight arteries).
Proliferative = straight tubular glands + mitoses (oestrogen).
Secretory = coiled “sawtooth” glands + glycogen vacuoles + stromal oedema (progesterone).
Sub-nuclear vacuoles (~day 16–17) are the first histological sign of ovulation.
Menstruation = corpus luteum regresses → hormone withdrawal → spiral-artery constriction & ischaemia.
Unopposed oestrogen → hyperplasia → endometrial carcinoma (postmenopausal bleeding).
Fibroid = leiomyoma (whorled, oestrogen-dependent); adenomyosis = endometrium within the myometrium.
